title: Two Ways to Play, and Two Verbs That Bend

lessons.title: giocare and suonare — the two verbs English calls "play"
lessons.gloss: the two verbs English calls "play" — one for games, one for instruments, and no relation between them

segments.text: English has one word for playing a game and playing an instrument. Italian has two unrelated ones, and picking the wrong one is the most recognisable mistake an English speaker makes.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: two words, not one

segments.text: giocare — to play a game, a sport, a match. suonare — to play an instrument; also, to ring or to sound.
The line is what you are doing, not the English word:

utterances: what you are doing: playing a game. Italian: giocare.
what you are doing: playing an instrument. Italian: suonare.
what you are doing: a bell ringing. Italian: suona.

segments.text: Chapter 19 gave you the frame — mi piace plus a dictionary form, as in mi piace leggere:
Mi piace giocare. — I like playing. Mi piace suonare. — I like playing music.
A grammatical tell too: giocare wants a before the game's name, while suonare takes the instrument bare.
Two roots, never near each other.
giocare from Latin iocārī, "to jest," from iocus, a joke. English took iocus as joke, and through French as jeopardy — jeu parti, "a divided game." Italian still calls a game il gioco.

suonare from Latin sonāre, "to sound," from sonus, a noise. That is English sound itself, plus sonata (from Italian: a thing sounded, against a cantata, a thing sung), resonate, unison, dissonant. And counterpoint — Italian contrappunto, note against note — carries the contrā of the last lesson's incontrare into music.
The split is no rule to memorise: two unrelated Latin words, covered in English by a single native verb.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the h that keeps a c hard

segments.text: Both are ordinary -are verbs — until the tu form of the first one.
gioco, giochi, gioca, suono, suoni, suona.

Gioco is JO-ko: the g is soft before i, the c hard before o. Now change the ending to -i: written gioci, that c would soften to JO-chee. Italian will not let a consonant shift because an ending did, so it spells in an h: giochi, JO-kee.
You have met that letter doing opposite work:

utterances: where: chiedere, mi chiamo, giochi. what the h does: keeps a c hard before e and i.
where: hanno against anno. what the h does: separates two identical sounds in writing.

segments.text: The second row is Chapter 14: hanno venti anni, where hanno ("they have") and anno ("year," from annus, the annus of annual) sound identical and only the silent h tells them apart.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Mi piace giocare." then "Mi piace suonare."]

segments.text: Which verb plays a match, and which an instrument? (Giocare; suonare.) Give each root and an English cousin. (Iocus becomes joke, jeopardy; sonus becomes sound, sonata.) Say you like playing music. (Mi piace suonare.) Give the tu form of giocare and the letter's two jobs. (Giochi — the h holds the c hard, as in chiedere; in hanno it separates the word from anno.)

lessons.title: ottenere — "to get," and a b that flattened into a t
lessons.gloss: to get, to obtain — a holding-verb, and a b that flattened into a t

segments.text: The last lesson was about doing — playing a game, playing an instrument. This one is about having. English get means almost anything; Italian has nothing of the sort, and for the sense that matters, coming to have a thing, the verb is this one.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the word

segments.text: ottenere — to get, to obtain, to come to have.
Line it up with what you have. Prendere seizes a thing, portare carries it. Ottenere obtains it: it was not lying there for the taking.
ottenere comes from Latin obtinēre: ob-, "toward, up against," plus tenēre, "to hold." To obtain is to get a hold on something:
obtain — the compound borrowed whole.
tenacious, tenant and tenure (a holding), tenet ("he holds"), tenor.
contain, retain, maintain — which Chapter 17 gave you as "hold in the hand."
English stacked prefixes on tenēre exactly as it stacked them on the last chapter's portāre: one Latin verb, a rack of prefixes.

Tenēre also explains Chapter 14, where Italian counted years with avere: Ho venti anni. Spanish says tengo veinte años, Portuguese tenho vinte anos, and both verbs are this same tenēre. Where Italian has its years, Spain and Portugal hold theirs — and English and German simply are twenty.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: bt lands on tt, and a stem that bends

segments.text: Obtinēre has a b and a t side by side, and Italian will not say them that way. It does to -bt- what it did to -ct- and -pt-: the first consonant flattens into the second.

The forms bend under stress: ottengo, ottieni, ottiene. A g surfaces in the io form; the stem's e breaks into ie in the other two. Where giocare spelled in an h to hold a consonant still, this verb lets the vowel move instead. The past is ordinary — ottenuto, regular the way portato was, so ho ottenuto. That -ngo is the shape Spanish shows in tengo.

segments.text: What two pieces make obtinēre, and name three English cousins? (Ob- plus tenēre; obtain, tenacious, tenant, maintain.) Why ottenere and not obtenere? (-bt- flattens to -tt-, as -ct- did in otto.) Give the singular forms and the participle, and the Chapter 20 participle it behaves like. (Ottengo, ottieni, ottiene; ottenuto, like portato.) Which Latin verb do Spanish tengo and Portuguese tenho come from? (Tenēre.)

lessons.title: rispondere — "to answer," which is "to pledge back"
lessons.gloss: to answer — literally "to pledge back", the other half of Chapter 19's asking

segments.text: Back to the -ere family: the present costs nothing new. Chapter 19 taught you to ask; this is the other half, and its root is about a promise, not speech.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the word

segments.text: rispondere — to answer. On the -ere pattern of leggo and chiedo: rispondo, rispondi, risponde.
One catch, mirroring one you own. Aspettare takes its object bare where English needs a preposition — aspetto Anna, "I wait for Anna." Rispondere demands an a where English wants none:
Rispondo a Marco. — I answer Marco.
rispondere from Latin respondēre: re-, "back," plus spondēre, "to pledge solemnly." An answer was a pledge given in return, and the English family is unexpectedly personal:
respond, response, responsible; correspond, "pledge together"; despond.
sponsor from spōnsor, who pledges for you.
spouse from spōnsus, spōnsa, "the promised one," and espouse.
Chiedere, with its hard ch, came from quaerere, "to seek." The asking-verb is a hunt; the answering-verb a promise.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the participle, and which past a story uses

segments.text: The participle is risposto — ho risposto, "I answered." Latin's was respōnsum, with the same -ns- as prehēnsum, and prehēnsum gave you preso: the n dropped, a plain -s- left. So this should be risposo. It is not. Risposto joins a small -ere band ending in -sto, with chiedere's chiesto — Chapter 17's principle over la mano: an "irregular" form is a regular one from a system you can no longer see.

Chapter 15's other past, the passato remoto — parlò, parlarono — is the one a story uses, because answering is what people do in stories. In Sicily and the south it is ordinary speech; in the north it retreated into books, as French shelved its passé simple.
giocare from iocus, "a jest" becomes joke, jeopardy — a game. suonare from sonus, "a noise" becomes sound, sonata, unison — an instrument. English merged them; Italian never did.
ottenere from ob- + tenēre, "hold toward" becomes obtain, tenant, retain, with -bt- landing where -ct- and -pt- did, and a bending stem: ottengo, ottieni, ottiene.
rispondere from re- + spondēre, "pledge back" becomes respond, sponsor, spouse.

The thread: Chapter 19 ended on verbs that reach, and on piacere, which reaches back from the thing to you. This chapter closes it: ottenere is the reach that lands, rispondere the return journey, giocare a reach for nothing at all.

Answer Marco. (Rispondo a Marco.) What did spondēre mean, and name three English cousins. (To pledge; respond, sponsor, spouse.) Give the participle and say why it is not risposo. (Risposto — the -sto band with chiesto, not the -so of preso.) Which Latin verbs sit under chiedere and ottenere, and where is the passato remoto everyday speech? (Quaerere; tenēre; the south.)
